newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists repeat pledge of no austerity.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists repeat pledge of no austerity.

text.p: France's Socialist party is sticking to its pledge that it will not impose austerity just to reduce the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, party spokesman Francois Hollande said on Monday.

But he declined to say exactly what the party would do if it won power after the second round of France's parliamentary election on Sunday and found, once in office, that French public finances were in a worse state than believed.

He also said that though the party was critical of the centre-right government's decision to transfer pension funds from France Telecom to the state budget to help meet the three percent deficit target this year, no decision had been made by the Socialists on whether it should be transferred back again.

"If was really necessary, it could be retained for a few years just to respect the (Maastricht treaty) criteria," he told a news conference. The pension fund money from France Telecom is for a total of 37.5 billion francs ($6.6 billion), or 0.45 percent of GDP. Any decision to return the funds would leave a big hole in budget deficit this year.
Hollande reiterated that the Socialist party believed in respecting Maastricht treaty convergence criteria, but was against "an arithmetical approach to three percent".
The party would carry out an audit of public finances if it won power to establish what needed to be done.
"Our position is not to impose austerity on the French people," he said.

He declined to say, however, whether the party would be willing to make spending cuts or increase taxes if public finances were much worse than thought, though said "some savings" might be possible on some spending.
The party had doubts that the picture of public finances painted by the government, which says France is on course to meet the Maastricht treaty deficit criterion, was correct, Hollande said.
But no-one believed that the total state deficit could be as high as four percent of gross domestic product.
The Socialist party has said it wants a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty and will seek negotiations with France's European partners if its deficit overshoots three percent.

Hollande also said the Socialist party planned to put the fight against unemployment -- through a cut in the working week, job schemes for young people and a boost to consumption -- at the heart of its campaign.
"If there has to be a change (in policy) it is in the fight against unemployment," he said.
-- Myra MacDonald, Paris Newsroom +33 1 42 21 53 81 ($ = 5.690 French Francs)
